extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (especially readers of Locke / early modern epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative and conceptual standards about human happiness, right and wrong judgment, liberty, and the nature/origin of complex ideas (mixed modes) from a philosophical treatise. Useful for philosophical analysis or pedagogy on judgment, action, and language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Every intelligent being really seeks happiness, which consists in the enjoyment of pleasure, without any considerable mixture of uneasiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is treated as the net enjoyment of pleasure over uneasiness; this grounding is used repeatedly to evaluate actions and choices (i.e., an action is good if it contributes to pleasure without significant uneasiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgment as cause of choosing misery
rubrics_metrics.description: No one chooses misery willingly, but only by wrong judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong judgment is identified with misreporting the comparative values of pleasures and pains; people only select harmful actions when they have misjudged the relevant pleasures/pains (not through sheer willing of misery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper comparison of present and future pleasures/pains
rubrics_metrics.description: When we compare present pleasure or pain with future (which is usually the case in most important determinations of the will), we often make wrong judgments: the present is apt to carry it; those at a distance are disadvantaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving present pleasures disproportionate weight simply because of temporal nearness. Example given: drinking now versus future sickness; the future, when it becomes present, will show its full dimensions and expose initial misjudgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological causes of mis-weighing present vs future
rubrics_metrics.description: The weak and narrow constitution of our minds: we cannot enjoy two pleasures at once; present pleasure fills the narrow soul and often excludes consideration of distant goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because present pleasure or pain dominates attention, decisions are frequently precipitate; to correct this, one must deliberately bring future goods into present consideration and counteract the mind's narrowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to undervalue absent/future good
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent good, especially if unfamiliar, seldom counterbalances present uneasiness; people lower its expected value because of doubts that it will match its reputation or previous experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating distant or unfamiliar pleasures, correct for undue skepticism about their eventual character (the author argues this is especially erroneous when applied to the happiness of another life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgment about consequences (two forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: As to things good or bad in their consequences, we judge amiss several ways: (1) judging that so much evil does not really depend on them as in truth there does; (2) judging that though the consequence be of that moment, yet it is not of that certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not under-estimate either the magnitude or the probability of consequences. It is irrational to risk a greater good for a lesser on uncertain guesses without proportionate examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of wrong judgment (information and attention failures)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) Ignorance — judging without informing oneself; (ii) Inadvertency — overlooking what one does know (precipitancy due to present passions); along with sloth, negligence, heat, fashion, and acquired dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective: use understanding and reason to search and consider fully before judging; guard against haste and omissions in the mental 'reckoning' of pros and cons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgment about what is necessary to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Men often take up with any pleasure at hand and, if they think they can be happy without some greater apparent good, it moves them not; they neglect goods or means necessary to real happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a particular apparent good is necessary to your happiness; do not omit essential means merely because they are unpleasant or remote in time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to change agreeableness/disagreeableness (habit and practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in a man’s power to change the pleasantness and unpleasantness that accompanies any sort of action: palates of the mind may be altered; use, practice, and custom can render initially disagreeable actions pleasant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To pursue necessary goods, one should employ consideration, trial, and habituation to acquire a taste or relish for useful (including virtuous) actions; examples include learning to like otherwise unpleasant but healthful foods and making virtue agreeable by practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference of vice to virtue as a manifest wrong judgment (infinite stakes argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the possibility of infinite happiness or misery after this life, it is a manifest wrong judgment to prefer short pleasures of a vicious life to the virtuous life that may bring everlasting bliss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When outcomes include potentially infinite rewards or punishments, prudence (expected-value reasoning) strongly favors the choice that secures the infinite good or avoids infinite harm; choosing otherwise is irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapitulation of liberty and will (liberty defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is a power to act or not to act, according as the mind directs. The WILL is a power to direct the operative faculties to motion or rest in particular instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That which determines the will is some present uneasiness accompanied with desire; freedom consists in the will being determined by one's own desire guided by one's own judgment (i.e., the will is not free if determined by anything but the agent's own desire guided by judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and list of original ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our original ideas, from whence all the rest are derived: EXTENSION, SOLIDITY, MOBILITY (from body); PERCEPTIVITY, MOTIVITY (from the mind); and also EXISTENCE, DURATION, NUMBER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These primary ideas are the building blocks for all other ideas; subsequent analysis and explanation reduce complex ideas to combinations of these simple ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and unity of mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed modes are complex ideas made of several simple ideas of different kinds (e.g., obligation, drunkenness, a lie); their unity comes from an act of the mind combining their parts, and the NAME given to that combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed modes are mental compositions rather than fixed real entities; a name commonly fixes the unity of a mixed mode and makes it a distinct idea in language and thought. Example analysis: the complex idea of a LIE is composed of articulate sounds, certain ideas in the speaker, words as signs, and those signs put otherwise than the ideas they stand for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three ways of acquiring mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: We get complex ideas of mixed modes: (1) by experience/observation of things; (2) by invention/voluntary composition of simple ideas in the mind; (3) by explication of names for actions or motions never seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many complex ideas are formed via language: explaining the constituent simple ideas of a word can convey the mixed mode to someone who has never directly observed it (e.g., murder, sacrilege, reprieve).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and naming determine which complex ideas are fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Names tie the parts of mixed modes into one idea; languages make certain collections of ideas into settled modes because those collections are frequently useful in a people’s life, leading to names that avoid long periphrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences between languages (words with no exact equivalents) reflect different habitual combinations of ideas; languages change as customs and opinions change because new combinations need names and old ones fall out of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among power, action, cause, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Power is the source from which action proceeds; when power exerts into act it is called CAUSE in the acting subject and EFFECT in the subject changed; EFFICACY is ACTION in the agent and PASSION in the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual clarity: analyze modes of action (e.g., consideration, assent, running, speaking, revenge, murder) as collections of simple ideas and distinguish who is cause/agent and who undergoes the effect/passion.
